notes.meaning: Adoni-zedek, the king of Jerusalem, learned that Joshua had captured and destroyed Jericho and Ai. He also heard that the people of Gibeon had made a peace treaty with Israel and now lived among them. Although his name meant 'lord of righteousness,' he chose to oppose God's work. The news filled him with deep anxiety because an important neighbor had changed sides.

The king and his citizens were terrified because Gibeon was a major city with brave and skilled fighters. Even though Gibeon was governed by elders rather than a king, it was as large and strong as a royal capital. The leaders of Jerusalem knew that if such a powerful city surrendered, their own defenses were in danger.

Adoni-zedek sent an urgent message to the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon. These four rulers controlled key southern territories and major trade routes. Jerusalem's king knew he could not face Israel alone, so he called on his neighbors to unite their strength.

Adoni-zedek urged the four kings to join him in attacking Gibeon for making peace with Joshua. By crushing Gibeon, the coalition hoped to punish their former allies and warn other cities not to surrender to Israel. When people turn to God, their former friends often turn against them.

The five Amorite kings gathered their armies and surrounded Gibeon to lay siege to the city. The Bible uses the name Amorites here as a general term for the strong peoples living in the southern hill country. Without knowing it, these kings gathered together so God could give Israel victory over all five at once.

The Gibeonites sent an urgent appeal to Joshua at his camp in Gilgal, pleading for swift help. They reminded Joshua of their covenant, asking him not to abandon them in their hour of danger. When hard times press in, believers can turn to God just as eagerly for rescue and protection.

Joshua marched out from Gilgal with his whole army, including his finest and bravest fighters. He took his covenant seriously and did not use Gibeon's past deceit as an excuse to break his promise. Keeping our word remains important even when it requires hard labor and personal risk.

The Lord spoke to Joshua and told him not to fear this large combined army. God promised that He had already handed the enemies over to Israel and that none of them could stand against him. God gives His promises to give us courage, not to make us lazy.

Joshua led his army on an uphill climb throughout the night and surprised the enemy at dawn. By marching fifteen to twenty miles in the dark, Israel struck before the Amorites were prepared for battle. Joshua showed that trusting God's promises goes hand in hand with doing our very best work.

The Lord threw the Amorite armies into total panic before the advancing Israelites. Israel crushed the enemy at Gibeon and chased the fleeing soldiers down the steep, rocky pass of Beth-horon toward Azekah and Makkedah. The victory belonged to God, who fought directly on behalf of His people.

As the enemy armies fled down the slope, the Lord sent a violent storm of massive hailstones upon them. The falling ice was aimed so precisely that it killed more enemies than the swords of Israel did, while leaving the Israelites unharmed. The Canaanites worshipped the skies, but God showed that nature serves only His commands.

Joshua spoke to the Lord before the entire army of Israel as the battle raged. Inspired by God, he boldly ordered the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon. Joshua knew that nightfall would allow the enemy to slip away, so he trusted God for more daylight to finish the job.

The sun stopped in the sky and the moon paused until Israel completed its victory over the five armies. This miraculous event was also recorded in the Book of Jashar, a well-known collection of ancient Hebrew poems. The Lord proved that the sun and moon, which the Canaanites worshipped, were completely under His control.

differ.view: Some evangelicals suggest that God provided extra light through unusual atmospheric conditions or shielded the army from scorching heat, rather than halting the rotation of the earth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars view the quotation from the Book of Jashar as poetic language celebrating a great victory, rather than a description of a physical alteration in nature.

notes.meaning: Scripture records that there was never another day like this one, when the Lord lengthened the daylight at the request of a man. The great wonder was not just the extended day, but the truth that God fought openly for His people. It shows that God listens with care to bold prayers offered in faith.

This statement looks ahead to the final outcome of the campaign, when Joshua and his army returned safely to the camp at Gilgal. The actual return did not happen that same day, since the pursuit and capture of the kings still had to be finished. Ancient writers often summarized the end of a matter before detailing the steps that led up to it.

The five Amorite kings escaped the battlefield and took refuge inside a cave near Makkedah. They had ridden out proudly to punish Gibeon, but now they cowered in the dark to save their own lives. People may try to flee from trouble, but no one can hide from the presence and judgment of God.

Word quickly reached Joshua that the five enemy rulers were hiding together in the cave at Makkedah. Finding them trapped in one place gave the Israelite army a great advantage. Joshua was able to manage the capture without letting it pull his troops away from the broader battle.

Joshua ordered large boulders rolled across the entrance of the cave and stationed guards to watch it. This smart tactic sealed the kings inside while using only a small number of soldiers. It kept the guards safe and allowed the rest of Israel's army to stay focused on the retreating enemy.

Joshua instructed his troops not to linger at the cave, but to press on and attack the rear of the fleeing enemy. He wanted to keep the Amorites from slipping behind the walls of their fortified cities, where they could recover and fight again. When God gives an opportunity, we should pursue it with diligence until the work is finished.

Joshua and the Israelite soldiers inflicted a crushing defeat on the Amorites until the enemy force was completely broken. Only a scattered few managed to escape into the safety of their walled towns. God was faithful to fulfill His promise that the enemy would not be able to stand before Israel.

The entire army returned safely to Joshua's camp at Makkedah without losing a man or suffering serious injury. The local inhabitants were so stunned and terrified by the outcome that no one dared say a single word against Israel. God granted His people complete peace and protection in the midst of their enemies.

After the pursuit was completed, Joshua commanded the soldiers to roll away the stones and bring the five kings out of the cave. The time had come for these rulers to face a public accounting for their defiance and hostility. God brings every ruler who opposes His will into open and righteous judgment.
